_comment: Per-question mapping + per-option rationale for the community mock exam (jtur671/gh-600-study-guide). Option order matches the source markdown (A, B, C, D). 'correct' holds zero-based option indexes.

why: More diff context is more output, not earlier insight. The complaint is that reviewers cannot see intent before the code exists, and a bigger diff arrives at the same time as the small one.
Correct. A structured plan published as a workflow artifact (or PR description) before any code is written is exactly the 'separate planning from execution' pattern. Reviewers validate intent first.
CODEOWNERS approvals gate the merge, which happens after the code already exists. It does not surface the agent's intent any earlier.
Making the agent read-only removes the capability entirely instead of making its reasoning visible. That solves the symptom by deleting the feature.
Correct. 'Planless execution' is the canonical anti-pattern in the Foundations module: the agent starts changing code without an inspectable approach, so reviewers only ever see the diff.
A read-only permissions block is least privilege done right, not an anti-pattern.
Attribution to the human who triggered the run is acceptable; the anti-pattern is having no attribution or audit trail at all.
Working on a protected feature branch is exactly the bounded, PR-based pattern the modules recommend.
Grouped logs improve readability but nothing gates the transition from planning to action, so an unreviewed plan still becomes code.
Correct. Plan artifact → human approval → action job → evaluation is the inspectable separation: each phase leaves durable evidence and execution cannot start until the plan is accepted.
Gating on `github.actor` is identity checking, not plan validation. Any admin-triggered run still executes an unreviewed plan.
`needs:` only enforces ordering. Sequential jobs with no approval gate still run straight through from plan to action.
Blanket approval on every PR is the 'governance fatigue' failure mode: reviewers rubber-stamp low-risk changes and stop reading the high-risk ones.
Time-of-day restrictions do not correlate with risk. A destructive change at 2am is as damaging as one at 2pm.
Correct. Risk-based autonomy — classify by operational, security, and compliance risk, then require approval only where risk is material — is the published guidance in the Governance module.
Isolating agents in a scratch repository removes the risk by removing the value. It does not let agents contribute to real work safely.
Console output scrolls away and is bound to a single run's retention. The modules explicitly recommend uploading artifacts precisely because logs are not durable enough.

Correct. A plan uploaded with `actions/upload-artifact` and linked from an 'Evidence' section in the PR is the canonical GitHub-native inspectable artifact: durable, traceable to a run and commit, reviewable in place.
External systems break the 'GitHub as system of record' model — the evidence is no longer attached to the change it justifies.
A source comment is not produced per run, so it cannot record what this particular execution intended or did.

Correct. Success criteria should be objective and enforceable: required checks pass, no new scanning alerts, and the PR template's required fields are complete. These map directly to status checks the platform can gate on.
A self-reported 'success' is the agent grading its own homework. The modules are explicit that evaluation must be grounded in system signals, not agent confidence.
Elapsed time measures speed, not whether the upgrade actually resolved the vulnerability.
Approving the description validates the narrative, not the change. 'CI passed' plus a good story is still not proof the intent was met.
A larger memory window may help the agent remember the plan, but nothing stops it acting when it diverges anyway. This is a hope, not a control.

Correct. Treat the plan as a contract: re-read it at the start of the action phase and abort when steps diverge. Validating plans (and gating action on that validation) is the published Domain 1 skill.
A more capable model reduces the frequency of divergence but does not detect or block it when it happens.
Retries are about transient failure recovery and are unrelated to plan/action divergence.
Memory is a separate concern (issues, PRs, instructions files). MCP is a tool-exposure protocol, not a memory store.
Correct. An MCP server exposes tools, APIs, or data sources to an AI client through one standardized protocol, so you do not build a bespoke integration per tool.
Execution still happens on GitHub Actions runners. MCP supplies tools to the agent; it does not host the run.
MCP describes tools and their invocation, not prompt templates.

Correct. When other agents in the same org work fine, the difference is org-level policy. Check whether 'Restrict MCP access to registry servers' is set to 'Registry only' and whether the server is in the registry.
Restarting the runner addresses transient infrastructure faults, not a policy block that would fail identically every time.
A timeout produces a cancelled run, not a refusal to invoke the server at all.
`GITHUB_TOKEN` governs GitHub API access for the workflow, not which MCP servers Copilot policy permits.
'Remote' describes where the server is hosted, not a universal replacement for every vendor's local server. Local MCP servers remain valid and are required for local-resource access.

Correct. The GitHub MCP server (hosted at https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/) exposes GitHub's own capabilities — repositories, issues, pull requests, code search — to MCP-capable clients. Remote is the recommended setup for most users in supported IDEs.
Outbound network control is the job of firewall/egress allow-listing in the agent's execution environment, not of the MCP server.
MCP has nothing to do with syncing Copilot subscription state.

11.stemOverride: Which of the following statements about MCP allow lists are true? (Select all that apply.)
why: True. That is precisely their purpose: an org or enterprise policy restricting which MCP servers agents may connect to.
False. An allow list decides *whether* a server may be used. Read/write capability comes from the tool configuration and the credentials the server is given — not from the allow list.

True. Enforcement is at the policy layer. With 'Registry only' selected, a server absent from the registry is blocked even if an agent config names it explicitly — and local servers must be listed with exactly matching IDs.
False. Allow lists and per-tool permissions are complementary layers. Being allowed to reach a server does not grant every tool on it.

Correct. Create a workflow file that triggers on the event (`on: pull_request`), set its `permissions:` block, and run the agent as a step — for example `npx @github/copilot-cli --agent <name> -p "..."`. The workflow becomes the execution boundary.
A webhook to an external endpoint moves execution off-platform, losing the workflow's permission scoping, logs, and artifacts.
CODEOWNERS routes review requests. It cannot execute anything.
`dependabot.yml` configures dependency update PRs only; it does not invoke arbitrary agents.
Read-only cannot push a branch or open a PR. The workflow would fail at the first write.
Correct. `contents: write` allows creating the branch and commits; `pull-requests: write` allows opening and updating the PR. That is the minimum for this task — nothing broader.
`write-all` grants far more than the task needs (packages, deployments, security events, and more) and violates least privilege.
`actions: write` manages workflow runs. It grants neither commit nor PR capability.
CODEOWNERS controls who reviews changed paths. It has no effect on outbound network calls.

Correct. Network isolation with an allow list of permitted outbound hosts is the environment-specific constraint control. GitHub Agentic Workflows apply the same defense-in-depth idea: network isolation plus allowlisted outbound access.
Secret scoping controls which credentials a job can read, not which hosts it may reach.
Branch protection governs merges into `main`; it says nothing about egress during a run.
Ten immediate retries on any error hammers a struggling service and will happily repeat a logic error ten times, compounding damage.
Correct. Bounded count, exponential backoff, idempotency on the underlying operation, and retrying only transient classes (network, rate limit) — that is the safe-retry shape the modules describe.
One retry then escalate is safe but wasteful: it pages a human for an ordinary transient blip that a second attempt would have cleared.
Disabling retries turns every transient network hiccup into a failed run and a human interruption.
A classic PAT with `repo` scope carries the user's access to *every* repository they can reach — the opposite of repository scoping.
Correct. The workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is minted per run and automatically scoped to the repository the workflow lives in, with capability further narrowed by the `permissions:` block.
An installation token granted org-wide reaches every repository in the installation, which is broader than the task requires.
An admin user's OAuth token is the widest option available and would let a mistake propagate across the whole organization.

Correct. Traceability needs three things together: what happened (run logs), who did it (commit attribution to the agent identity), and why (decisions recorded in the PR). All three live in GitHub and survive the run.
An email is a one-time notification, not a durable record attached to the change. You cannot reconstruct a decision trail from an inbox.
Disabling logs removes the primary forensic surface. Missing evidence is treated as a failure in the Governance module.
Private chat is off-platform, unattributed to the commit, and typically outside retention and audit policy.
Re-injecting stable facts into every prompt is short-term memory doing long-term memory's job: costly, easy to forget, and invisible to reviewers.

Correct. Stable, project-wide guidance belongs in a durable repository artifact such as `.github/copilot-instructions.md` or `AGENTS.md`, where it is versioned, reviewable, and picked up on every invocation.
Secrets are for credentials. Instructions are not sensitive and secrets are not designed to be read as context.
Hard-coding instructions into a binary makes them unreviewable and unchangeable without a release.
A bigger context window lets you load more irrelevant text. It raises cost and does not fix dilution.

Correct. 'Scope memory to task-relevant information' is the published skill: load only what affects this task's outcome — requirements, constraints, decisions, validation approach — and leave the rest out.
Retries re-run the same over-loaded context and produce the same diluted answer.
Disabling memory removes the requirements and prior decisions the agent needs. The fix is selectivity, not amnesia.
A longer timeout reduces how often the run is cut short but does nothing to make the next run resume rather than restart.

Correct. Durable state — PR description checkboxes, commits already pushed, workflow run results in the Checks tab — lets the agent open the existing PR, see what is done, and continue from the latest state.
Concurrency settings control whether runs overlap or cancel each other. They do not carry progress between runs.
Runner size affects speed, not the ability to resume from persisted state.
Slower responses are a performance symptom. Drift is about correctness of alignment, not latency.

Correct. Context drift is when the agent's actions no longer align with the original goal or prior decisions — typically because it is working from stale or cached context rather than current repository state.
A long prompt template is a cost and context-budget problem, not drift.
Actions minutes consumption is a billing concern, unrelated to alignment.
Priority rules pick a winner without making the two views consistent. The losing agent still holds a wrong picture of the world.

Correct. Define a single source of truth per information type and serialize writes to it. In GitHub that means the issue holds requirements and the PR holds decisions and progress — every tool reads and updates the same artifact rather than keeping private copies.
Separate repositories eliminate the collision by eliminating the collaboration. The agents still need shared state.
Shrinking memory does not stop two agents from independently forming conflicting private views.
Automated. Code scanning (CodeQL) produces alerts and check runs without human involvement.
Automated. Secret scanning — and push protection — generate signals mechanically.
Automated. Dependency review runs as a check on the PR and blocks known-vulnerable dependencies.
Not automated. Reviewer commentary is a qualitative human signal. It matters for evaluation, but the question asks specifically about automated scanning signals.
Asking humans to read more carefully is a process wish, not an enforceable control. It fails exactly when the team is busy.
Correct. Turn the operational constraint into a machine-checkable signal: run the benchmark in CI, fail the job past a threshold, and make it a required status check so a regressing PR cannot merge.
Blocking the agent from critical-path files removes capability instead of adding a gate, and humans regress performance too.
Raising test timeouts hides the regression by making the slow code pass.
A reasoning error is a wrong plan or wrong inference — misreading requirements, choosing invalid logic. Here the plan may have been fine; the execution reached for the wrong instrument.
Correct. Tool misuse covers calling the wrong tool, or calling the right tool incorrectly — misconfigured workflows, wrong commands, failing to trigger a workflow properly.
Context issues are missing, stale, or conflicting information. Nothing in the trace points to bad inputs.
A network failure is an environment fault, not a decision the agent made.
Correct. When the root cause is an ambiguous tool description, the fix is to refine tool usage and access: clarify the description, add usage examples, and rename anything ambiguous.
A larger token budget does not disambiguate a description the model is reading correctly and interpreting reasonably.
Removing the tool discards capability the agent legitimately needs. Tune before you amputate.
Changing model provider is an expensive shot in the dark for a problem you have already localized to your own configuration.

Correct. Aligning evaluation with development intent means judging agent work by the same signals a human contributor is judged on — tests, lint, security scans, review feedback — so agents stay accountable to the team's real quality bar.
Agent-only metrics such as tool calls per task measure mechanism, not outcome. Optimizing them can actively diverge from what the team wants.
Removing review from agent PRs breaks the contributor model and deletes the qualitative signal.
Self-reported confidence is the one signal the modules explicitly warn against: evaluation must be grounded in system signals, not the agent's confidence.
Yes. Workflow run logs show what executed and where it errored.
Yes. The structured plan captures intent, so you can compare what was supposed to happen with what did.
Yes. The execution trace shows the ordered tool calls, which is how you spot tool misuse.
Yes. Uploaded artifacts hold intermediate state and evaluation output, and remain available after logs scroll away. All four are named diagnostic surfaces.
Correct. Team conventions are stable, project-wide knowledge, so they belong in repository instructions. Revising instructions is the first tuning lever for reasoning errors.
Raising autonomy lets the agent apply the wrong style faster and with less oversight.
A retry loop re-runs the same misunderstanding; it treats a knowledge gap as a transient fault.
Reducing memory removes context. The problem is that the correct convention was never recorded anywhere durable.
Simultaneous execution with a merge at the end is fan-out/fan-in — in GitHub Actions, parallel jobs plus a `needs:` job that fans in.
Correct. In the supervisor pattern one agent dispatches sub-tasks to workers and reviews their outputs, holding responsibility for allocation and acceptance.
Two agents arguing with a third arbitrating is the debate/critic pattern, used to resolve contradictory outputs.
A fixed ordered chain is the sequential pipeline pattern (planner → coder → reviewer).
Three agents writing to `main` share one execution context — interleaved commits, ambiguous ownership, and no PR boundary to review at.
Correct. Isolation is the precondition for safe parallelism: a dedicated branch per agent (`agent/dependency/<ticket>`), non-overlapping path scopes, and conflict detection at the PR layer.
Serializing works but throws away the throughput you wanted. Isolation lets you keep the parallelism.
Runner size is a performance dial and has no bearing on whether two agents collide on the same file.
Auto-merging both guarantees the semantic conflict lands in `main`, where it is most expensive to unpick.

Correct. Resolve conflicts intentionally: a reconciler with a defined arbitration rule, or human-in-the-loop review once disagreement passes a threshold. Without arbitration, whichever PR merges first simply wins by timing.
Rejecting both discards work and does not decide which approach was right.
A force-push destroys one agent's history and its audit trail, and still leaves the conflict undecided.
Correct. Post-hoc analysis needs a linked record: a top-level orchestration artifact tying every sub-agent run together with decisions logged at each handoff, so you can replay who did what and why.
A single exit summary tells you the ending, not the sequence of decisions that produced it.
Debug output kept on the runner is discarded with the runner. Nothing durable survives.
A Slack thread is off-platform, unattributed to runs and commits, and outside retention policy.
Letting a stalled agent run indefinitely burns budget and blocks downstream fan-in jobs forever.
Correct. Detect the stall with `timeout-minutes`, mark it failed, and route to a fallback: rerun the sub-agent in isolation, use an alternative, or escalate to a human with a concise summary.
More CPU does not help an agent that is stuck rather than slow.
Cancelling all three throws away the two runs that are working fine.
An immediate swap changes behavior for in-flight work with no evidence that the replacement is equivalent.
Correct. Shadow mode — run the new agent alongside the incumbent, compare outputs, grant no merge authority until parity is confirmed — adds the agent without disrupting active workflows.
Weekend-only scheduling limits exposure by clock time, not by risk, and gives you a thin, unrepresentative sample.
Disabling the incumbent for a week removes the baseline you need to compare against, and leaves no fallback if the new agent misbehaves.
Deleting configuration and runs destroys exactly the evidence compliance review depends on. Note that deleted workflow artifacts cannot be restored.

Correct. Retire while preserving auditability: the config stays in git history, runs and artifacts are retained under the retention policy, and the retirement decision is documented in a governance record.
Moving runs to unlinked external storage severs evidence from the changes it explains and usually falls outside the audit log.
Disabling logging protects nothing about the past and destroys the trail going forward.
Formatting a markdown file is the low-risk, fully reversible tier — a candidate for full automation.
Renaming a private variable in test code is contained and reversible; PR plus required checks is proportionate.
Correct. Changes under `.github/workflows/` that deploy to production are the classic 'small diff, big consequence' area — treat as high or critical risk and require explicit human authorization.
Commenting on an issue changes no code and no system state.
Correct. The `permissions:` block is the platform primitive for least privilege at execution time. Default to `contents: read` at workflow level and elevate only on the job that must write.
A Slack announcement is documentation of intent, not a technical control. The Governance module is blunt: if the platform cannot enforce it, it will be bypassed.
A pinned issue describes expected behavior. It cannot constrain a token.
A README note is 'controls in docs only' — the named anti-pattern.
Branch protection on `main` gates merges. It does not gate what happens at deploy time, and it would add friction to every routine PR.

Correct. An environment with required reviewers pauses the deploy job until a human approves, and can restrict production secrets to that environment — targeted oversight exactly at the high-impact decision point.
CODEOWNERS on all of `src/` taxes every ordinary change while still not gating the deployment itself.
There is no such repository setting.
Yes. Requiring approval only where changes are irreversible or compliance-sensitive concentrates human attention where it buys real safety.
Yes. Path-scoped CODEOWNERS routes review to people with context instead of taxing everyone on everything.
No. Two reviewers on a documentation typo is approval theater: it adds friction and trains reviewers to stop reading.
Yes. Environment protection rules gate production while dev and staging flow freely — velocity preserved, risk still gated.

Correct. Defense in depth for an irreversible change: CODEOWNERS review of the migration itself, an environment gate with required reviewers at the deploy, and a plan artifact reviewed before the action job runs. Layered controls, each catching what the others miss.
A retry loop makes an irreversible destructive operation happen repeatedly. This is the worst possible answer here.
A longer timeout gives the destructive operation more time to complete. It adds no oversight.
'Revert later' does not apply to irreversible changes — a dropped column takes the data with it.
